title: Komm mal her! Der Imperativ
summary: Give commands the friendly German way — the du/ihr/Sie imperative and the little softeners that keep it polite

blocks.title: Der du-Befehl: einfach das -st wegwerfen
blocks.body: To give a command to a friend, take the **du-form**, drop the **-st** ending *and* the pronoun *du*: *du kommst* → **Komm!**, *du machst* → **Mach!**. If the stem ends in *-t* or *-d* (or an awkward cluster), keep a soft **-e** so it's sayable: *du wartest* → **Warte!**, *du öffnest* → **Öffne!**. Separable verbs split as always — the prefix flies to the end: *du hörst zu* → **Hör zu!**
blocks.callout: German commands sound blunt on paper but warm in a café. The softeners on the next card fix the tone.

blocks.title: Die Weichmacher: mal, doch, bitte
blocks.body: A bare imperative can sound barked. Germans soften it with tiny particles: **mal** (just, briefly), **doch** (go on), **bitte** (please). *Komm!* is an order; **Komm mal!** is a nudge; **Komm doch mal her!** is warm and inviting. Stack them — *mal* and *doch* together are extra gentle.
blocks.callout: *Setz dich doch!* = „Do have a seat.” Same verb, zero bossiness.

blocks.prompt: Your friend is dawdling and you want to say „Wait!”. Which is the correct du-command?
blocks.explain: *Warte!* — drop the *-st* and the pronoun. You keep the *-e* here because the stem *wart-* ends in *-t*, otherwise it's a tongue-twister.

pairs.right: Kommen Sie mit! — to a stranger (Sie)
pairs.note: *du*: drop *-st* and the pronoun. *Sie*: keep the full *-en* form and put **Sie** right after the verb.
The reflexive switches too: *dich* → *sich*. Keep the register consistent across the whole sentence.

blocks.prompt: Tell a friend „Listen!” using the separable verb *zuhören*.
blocks.hint: Drop the -st, and the prefix zu- lands at the end.
blocks.explain: *Hör zu!* — the separable prefix *zu* jumps to the end, exactly like in a normal main clause (*du hörst zu*).

blocks.title: Zwei Sonderfälle: Gib! und Sei!
blocks.body: Strong verbs that flip **e→i/ie** in the du-form keep the flip and drop the *-e*: *du gibst* → **Gib!**, *du nimmst* → **Nimm!**, *du liest* → **Lies!**. But an **a→ä** switch does **not** carry over: *du fährst* → **Fahr!** (never *Fähr*). And *sein* is its own animal: **Sei ruhig!** / **Seien Sie ruhig!**

blocks.scene: Lena spots you across the street and waves you over — imperatives flying.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.nl: Ey, komm mal her! Guck mal, was ich gefunden habe.
lines.en: Hey, come here a sec! Look what I found.
lines.spotlight: *Komm mal her!* and *Guck mal!* — softened commands, the way friends actually talk.

lines.speaker: You
lines.nl: Warte, ich komme. Pass auf, ein Fahrrad!
lines.en: Wait, I'm coming. Watch out, a bike!

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.nl: Ups, danke. Setz dich kurz, ich erzähl dir was.
lines.en: Oops, thanks. Sit down a sec, I'll tell you something.

lines.speaker: You
lines.nl: Okay, aber mach schnell — ich habe echt Hunger.
lines.en: Okay, but be quick — I'm really hungry.

lines.speaker: Lena
lines.nl: Quatsch, komm, ich geb dir einen Kaffee aus. Sei nicht so ungeduldig!
lines.en: Nonsense, come on, coffee's on me. Don't be so impatient!
lines.spotlight: *Sei nicht so…!* — the irregular imperative of *sein*.

blocks.prompt: Write three friendly commands for a friend (use *mal* or *doch* so they sound warm, not bossy). Then write one polite Sie-command for a stranger — say, asking someone to wait a moment.
